rationale: 106.13 is the rule written specifically for Drain Power: it empties the first player's pool and moves the mana lost that way to the other player. Kruphix replaces the loss with the mana becoming colorless, and a replaced event never happens (614.1a defines 'instead' effects as replacements, 614.6 states the original event never occurs), so nothing is lost and nothing is added.

The attacker controls all four triggers and puts them on the stack in any order he chooses (603.3b), and each trigger reads the Beastmaster's power only when it resolves (608.2h), which is what lets the pumped values compound to 49 total.

107.1b is the only rule needed: a game value such as power can be less than zero, but a calculation that determines the result of an effect yields zero when it would be negative, so the +X/+X is +0/+0.

601.2f states the total cost is the alternative cost plus any additional costs, making both the Dream Halls discard and the reveal parts of the cost; 601.2h states the player pays all costs in any order, which is the actual answer.

Morph and madness each let you cast the card for an alternative cost (702.37a, 702.35a), and only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell as it's cast (118.9a), so the morph cost isn't available. The closing point that spells can be cast during the cleanup step comes from 514.3a (priority round during cleanup) or 608.2g (casting during resolution).

Both Auras' control-changing effects live in layer 2 (613.1b); applying Lay Claim's effect changes what Corrupted Conscience's effect does, which is the definition of dependency (613.8a); and the dependent effect waits until after the one it depends on (613.8b), reversing timestamp order.

111.8 states a token that has left the battlefield can't come back and stays where it is, which is why the exiled token never returns; 111.7/704.5d state that a token outside the battlefield ceases to exist as a state-based action.

510.1a states an attacking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power (so the blocker's toughness is irrelevant to the amount dealt), and 702.15b states lifelink damage also causes its source's controller to gain that much life.

712.21 states that when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves and two cards are put into the new zone, which is why the exiled objects are Midnight Scavengers and Graf Rats; 712.4b/701.42a establish that the combined back face only exists as a permanent on the battlefield.

607.2a links the exile ability to the ability that refers to 'the exiled card', so the reference works regardless of what the card currently is; 208.3 states a noncreature object not on the battlefield has power or toughness only if printed on it, so the animated-land card in exile has none and the bonus is +0/+0.

201.4c states directly that a player may choose a flip card's alternative name, and that the card's characteristics as modified by its alternative characteristics are used to check any required qualities.

708.4 states effects that care about a spell's characteristics see only the face-down spell's characteristics, so Possibility Storm sees a creature spell; 708.9 states a face-down spell moving off the stack is revealed, which is why the card sits face up (and non-creature) in exile.

The answer rests entirely on ordering the simultaneous triggers freely (603.3b) and on each trigger determining the creature's power only as it resolves (608.2h), which is what allows the counters to compound.

116.2d states that paying to ignore a static ability's effect (Leonin Arbiter's) is a special action that can only be taken when a player has priority, and 117.3b establishes priority only comes back after the ability has finished resolving, so there's no window to pay while the ability resolves.

704.5q states that a permanent with both +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters has equal numbers of each removed as a state-based action, and it says 'a permanent', not 'a creature', which covers the animated land.

406.3 states exiled cards are kept face up by default and may be examined by any player at any time; 608.2c states the ability's instructions are followed in the order written, so the pile is exiled (and visible) before the search of the other pile happens.
700.3d states a pile can contain zero objects, so the un-exiled pile being empty is legal; 701.24d states the library is shuffled even when the set of objects being shuffled into it is empty.
116.2f states the suspend special action can be taken only if the player could begin to cast that card by putting it on the stack, which is exactly the answer.

Permission to play the exiled card comes from Act on Impulse itself; the only rules content in the answer is the land-play limit, stated independently by 116.2a (once per turn by default), 305.2a (compare lands playable to lands already played) and 305.2b (can't play if the limit is reached).

305.2 states one land per turn normally and that continuous effects may increase that number (Oracle of Mul Daya raising it to two); 305.2a/305.2b state the comparison is against lands already played this turn, which blinking the Oracle doesn't reset.

Same as rg29: 305.2 gives the default of one land play modified upward by a continuous effect, and 305.2a/305.2b state the limit is checked against lands already played this turn, so a new Oracle grants no extra play.

The attacker orders his own simultaneous attack triggers (603.3b), each trigger reads the board only as it resolves so the tokens count or don't (608.2h), and Nobilis of War's static ability isn't locked in and applies to whatever creatures are attacking at any moment (611.3a).

113.7a states a triggered ability exists on the stack independently of its source and removal of the source doesn't affect it; 603.4/608.2a state the intervening-if condition is rechecked on resolution, and five other Mountains are still there, so the damage happens.

Both 603.4 and 608.2a independently state that a trigger with an intervening 'if' clause rechecks the condition as it resolves and is removed from the stack doing nothing if the condition is false, which is the whole answer once one Mountain is gone.

305.7 states that setting a land's subtype to a basic land type removes its old land types and rules-text abilities and grants the corresponding mana ability, which is all Blood Moon does; 205.1a states removing or replacing an object's subtype doesn't affect its card types, so it remains an artifact for Ensoul Artifact.

303.4e states an Aura's controller is separate from the enchanted object's controller; 110.2 independently states a permanent's controller is the player under whose control it entered the battlefield. Either establishes that the Aura entered under the caster's control, so the constellation trigger sees an enchantment entering under their control.

508.1f states the active player taps the chosen creatures as part of declaring attackers and that tapping isn't a cost; 508.1h/508.1j state the costs to attack are determined and paid at later steps of the same turn-based action, so the Myr is tapped regardless.

611.3c states a static ability's continuous effect applies simultaneously with the permanent entering, and 603.10 states trigger conditions are checked against objects as they exist immediately after the event, so control has already changed when the trigger is checked; 603.3a states the trigger is controlled by whoever controlled its source at that moment.

Same shape as rg39: the control-changing continuous effect applies as Volition Reins enters (611.3c) and trigger conditions are evaluated against the post-event game state (603.10), so the constellation ability triggers under the new controller per 603.3a.

601.2d states the division among targets is announced as the spell is cast, and 602.2b states rules 601.2b-i apply identically to activating an ability, so the damage division is locked in at activation and later power changes don't alter it.

704.5f states a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action (Mikaeus with X=0 has base 0/0); 704.5j states the legend rule applies only to legendary permanents with the same name controlled by the same player.

201.5 states text that refers to the object it's on by name means just that object, so the return ability keys off this permanent, not any card named Lunarch Inquisitors; 712.18 states a transforming double-faced permanent doesn't become a new object, so Moonmist flipping it isn't a leaves-the-battlefield event.

800.4a states that when a player leaves the game, effects giving them control of objects end; 603.10f states abilities that trigger when a player loses the game look back in time (so the trigger is controlled by the leaving player); 800.4d states a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game is never put on the stack.

704.5a/104.3b state a player at 0 or less life loses; 704.3 states state-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, which is after the original spell finishes resolving; 800.4a states objects on the stack controlled by the departing player that aren't cards (the copy) cease to exist.

608.2n states an instant or sorcery is put into its owner's graveyard only as the final part of its resolution, and 404.1 independently states a spell goes to the graveyard once it has finished resolving; either shows the spell never reaches a graveyard for Dryad Militant's replacement to catch.

Identical reasoning to rg47: the spell is only put into the graveyard as the last part of resolution (608.2n, restated by 404.1), so returning itself to hand mid-resolution means Dryad Militant's exile replacement never applies.

110.1 states a permanent is a card or token on the battlefield, so a manifested instant is a permanent while it's there; 400.6 states replacement effects for a zone change are applied to the move based on the object as it exists before the event, so Samurai of the Pale Curtain's effect applies and exiles it.

708.2a states a face-down permanent is a 2/2 creature with no text or subtypes, so the manifested card is a creature and not an instant or sorcery while on the battlefield; 400.6 states the replacement effects applied to the move are checked against the object as it exists before the event, so Dryad Militant's effect doesn't apply.

708.2a states the manifested card is a face-down 2/2 creature with no text, so Legacy Weapon's own replacement ability doesn't exist while it's on the battlefield; 614.4 states replacement effects must exist before the event to apply and can't go back in time.
Same as rg51: face down, Ugin's Nexus has no text (708.2a), and a replacement effect that didn't exist immediately before the event can't apply to it (614.4), so it goes to the graveyard.

105.3 states a color-changing effect replaces all previous colors, so the creature is mono-red and no longer blue; 608.2b states target legality is rechecked on resolution and an illegal target means the spell is removed from the stack and doesn't resolve.

704.5a/104.3b state that a player at 0 or less life loses the game; 704.3/117.5 state that this check happens the next time a player would receive priority, i.e. after the spell has fully resolved and returned itself to hand.

The answer is entirely card-text arithmetic (damage equals the number of cards revealed, and revealing extra copies of the card doesn't add damage). No Comprehensive Rules chunk states this; there is no rules question being resolved.

613.1f states ability-removing effects apply in layer 6, so Turn to Frog strips Grothama of its abilities and it grants nothing; 201.5a states that when an ability grants another object an ability that refers to the granting source by name, that name means only that specific object, so only the Sakashima copy's granted ability points at itself.

201.5a states the granted ability's name reference points at the specific object that granted it, so the Gore Swine's ability refers to Lazav; 702.11b states hexproof only stops it being the target of opponents' spells and abilities, and fighting via this ability doesn't target.

800.4a states all objects owned by the departing player leave the game, which removes Grasp of Fate from the battlefield; 610.3 states an 'exile until [event]' effect creates a second one-shot effect returning the object immediately after that event, with no triggered ability involved, so the Reaver comes back.

800.4a states all objects owned by the leaving player leave the game, so Icy Prison leaves the battlefield; 800.4d states a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game is never put on the stack, so its leaves-the-battlefield return ability never resolves.

800.4a states all objects owned by the leaving player leave the game, so the Gorger leaves the battlefield; 603.10a states leaves-the-battlefield abilities look back in time, so Dual Nature (controlled by a player still in the game) sees the creature that was there and triggers.

702.89a states umbra armor replaces the destruction of the enchanted permanent by destroying the Aura instead; 701.8a states destroying a permanent means moving it to its owner's graveyard, so the graveyard move is contained within the destroy event; 616.1g states an effect applying to a contained event can't be chosen until the effect applying to the outer event has been chosen, forcing umbra armor to apply first.

701.44a states that exploring reveals the top card and, if a land isn't revealed, a +1/+1 counter goes on the exploring permanent, which is what happens when nothing can be revealed; 704.5b/104.3c state the loss condition is specifically attempting to draw from an empty library, not any other action.
